idiom_name: func(yield func(T) bool) as iter.Seq[T], driven by for range
implementation_notes: Go 1.23 makes a lazy sequence an ordinary function: an iterator passes successive elements to a yield callback, stops when yield returns false, and for-range drives it, so an unbounded or generated sequence is bounded by demand (the iter package defines Seq/Seq2 plus Pull for the pull-shaped view). The standard library has no memoizing lazy collection - iterators are single-use and recompute on every call - so caching requires an explicit closure or materializing with slices.Collect; the classic loop over a concrete slice stays preferable when all elements are needed anyway.
pitfalls: The yield contract is mandatory: a callback that returns false means the iterator must return immediately, and an iterator that keeps producing after being stopped wastes work and can leak goroutines.

Iterators are single-use by convention - calling range twice over one stored Seq value works only because range re-invokes the function; sharing a partially consumed iterator between goroutines races.
Blocking inside yield (network, locks) blocks the producer's goroutine, and a channel- or lock-based source can deadlock when the consumer stops early without signalling.

variants.name: Closure pull-iterator (pre-1.23 classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The long-standing Go idiom for a lazy sequence is a closure that captures the cursor state and returns the next element with an ok flag, so consumers drive demand with a plain for loop and a false return means exhaustion; it compiles on every Go version and keeps destruction deterministic (the captured state dies with the closure). It lacks range support and needs an explicit stop method when the source is a resource that must be closed before exhaustion, so use iter.Seq on modern toolchains and keep a close/error path visible.
pitfalls: Captured state is shared mutable state: calling the closure from two goroutines races, and an abandoned closure that holds a file/connection has no close hook.
There is no standard protocol, so every package invents its own next signature and combinators cannot be shared across libraries.
Termination is signalled by the zero value plus false, which silently conflates 'empty element' with 'done' for types where the zero value is meaningful.

variants.name: Goroutine plus channel generator
variants.idiom_name: goroutine writing into an unbuffered channel, cancelled by context
variants.implementation_notes: A goroutine producing elements into a channel gives a lazy sequence that also crosses goroutine boundaries: the consumer ranges over the channel and each receive pulls one element, which is convenient when production is I/O-bound or parallel. It is the most expensive realization - a goroutine per sequence plus channel hand-off per element - and the one with the worst failure mode, because a producer blocked on send is never collected when the consumer stops unless it selects on a done/context channel; use it when concurrency is the point, not merely for laziness.
pitfalls: A producer blocked on send leaks the goroutine (and everything it captured) forever when the consumer abandons the channel; every generator needs a done/context path.
Per-element channel hand-off costs a scheduling round-trip, making this the slowest realization for cheap elements; buffering trades memory for throughput.
Channels have no notion of a lazy cache: values pulled and discarded are gone, so shared or repeated traversal needs a different structure.
